sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has emerged as a promising treatment for hematologic malignancies, offering significant therapeutic benefits. However, this therapy is also associated with adverse effects such as cytokine release syndrome and Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS), which can lead to severe neurological symptoms. The pathophysiology of ICANS remains unclear but is believed to involve immune-mediated inflammation in the brain. This study investigates the potential of S100, a protein marker associated with blood-brain barrier integrity, as an early indicator of ICANS.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We retrospectively analyzed daily blood samples for S100 levels in patients undergoing CAR T-cell therapy, correlating these levels with the onset and severity of ICANS.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The results show that S100 levels significantly increased in patients who developed ICANS, with a positive correlation between the duration of elevation and the severity of the neurological symptoms.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: These findings suggest that S100 may serve as a useful biomarker for early detection of ICANS and could potentially guide therapeutic interventions. However, further studies are needed to fully understand its prognostic value in this context.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Recently, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has gained widespread application for hematologic diseases like lymphoma, leukemia, and myeloma [1–3]. In principle, this new kind of therapy uses genetically reprogrammed T cells of the patient to recognize and attack the cancer cells [4, 5].

Despite great success and comparatively better tolerability compared to alternative forms of treatment such as transplantation, CAR T-cell therapy also has some side effects such as neutropenia due to the preceding lymphodepleting chemotherapy, cytokine release syndrome, and the immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) [6]. The latter can lead to symptoms such as confusion, delirium, seizures, and other neurological issues. While the exact cause of ICANS is not fully understood, it is believed to be related to the immune response triggered by the CAR-T cells, leading to inflammation in the brain. In addition to symptomatic treatment, depending on the degree of ICANS, treatment consists of corticosteroids and anakinra, an Interleukin 1 receptor antagonist. The time of onset of ICANS can vary and is often preceded by cytokine release syndrome just a few days after CAR T-cell administration. Due to the neurological nature and sometimes severe course of ICANS, we routinely check a blood marker called S100 in all patients undergoing CAR T-cell therapy at our institution as described earlier [7]. It refers to a group of proteins that occur in various tissues of the body, including the nervous system. The S100 protein family serves as important biomarkers assessed via blood tests, particularly in neurology and oncology. In neurology, elevated S100 levels may indicate brain or spinal cord damage due to conditions like strokes, injuries, or neurodegeneration. In oncology, S100 measurements are crucial for diagnosing and monitoring melanomas. Additionally, S100 proteins are significant markers of blood-brain barrier integrity and have various biological roles, including calcium binding and modulation of cellular functions such as proliferation and apoptosis [8, 9]. They also facilitate neuron-glial cell interactions and indicate tissue damage. To explore the relationship between S100 levels and ICANS, we retrospectively analyzed the daily blood levels S100 in our patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy, aiming to uncover the correlation with clinical manifestations of ICANS.

sec.title: Materials/Subjects and Methods
sec.p: We retrospectively analyzed patients diagnosed with relapsed or refractory hematological malignancies who underwent CAR T-cell therapy at our institution from May 1 to November 1, 2024. Inclusion criteria comprised adults aged 18 years and older, with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–2, who provided written informed consent for chemotherapy and CAR T-cell therapy at our institution. Patients with significant comorbidities or those receiving concurrent immunosuppressive therapy were excluded from the study. The patient characteristics are displayed in Table 1.

sec.p: A baseline value of S100 was determined by a blood sample before the start of CAR T-cell therapy. Subsequently, daily blood samples were collected post-infusion until discharge to monitor the levels of this marker. S100 was quantified using electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA/Roche Diagnostics), and the results were expressed as µg/L.

Clinical assessments for ICANS were performed daily according to the ASTCT consensus guidelines [10]. The severity of ICANS was classified into grades 1–4 based on clinical symptoms, including headache, confusion, and seizures. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate whether changes in the levels of S100 correlated with the onset and severity of ICANS. Statistical analyses were conducted using the python modules scipy, matplotlib, numpy, and pandas. Comparisons were calculated using either the Pearson correlation coefficient or Mann-Whitney U test. p values <0.05 were considered as statistically significant.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated a total of 18 patients undergoing CAR T-cell therapy at our institution from May to November 2024. Before CAR T-cell therapy all patients had blood levels of S100 in the normal range (<0.105 µg/L). Later on 7 (38%) of these patients developed ICANS. The entire subpopulation of patients suffering from ICANS exhibited a significant increase in the blood marker. The increase in S100 levels was found to be statistically significant when compared with both baseline measurements within the group (p < 0.0023) and with the levels in patients not suffering from ICANS (p < 0.00022). We also observed a positive correlation between the duration of marker elevation and the occurrence of the side effect, with statistical analysis confirming this relationship (Pearson-correlation coefficient = 0.84, p = 0.038), suggesting that longer durations of elevation are associated with an increased likelihood of the side effect.

The increase in the blood marker was observed to last for an average of 6.5 days, occurring from 1.17 days before the onset of symptoms of ICANS to 2.5 days after. The peak elevation of the marker reached an average increase of 11-fold above baseline levels. Figure 1 depicts the aggregated number of patients with elevated S100 level, the aggregated number of patients suffering from ICANS, and the mean S100 level over time.

caption.p: Aggregated (sum of) patients with elevated S100 and patients suffering from ICANS as well as the mean S100 level over time, respectively.

sec.p: Following the initiation of therapy, a reduction in the blood marker was observed in all of our patients, which correlated with their clinical response to treatment. These findings suggest that the blood marker not only serves as a potential early indicator of disease onset but also as a possible predictor of treatment efficacy.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: CAR T-cell therapy has significantly advanced the treatment of hematologic malignancies but is associated with serious side effects, including Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS). The exact cause of ICANS remains unclear and treatment is often of limited benefit to patients with neurotoxicity [11, 12].

In this retrospective analysis, we examined the relationship between blood levels of the S100 protein and the onset of ICANS in patients receiving CAR-T therapy. S100 is a marker of blood-brain barrier dysfunction, which is linked to neurological damage. Our results show that S100 levels significantly increased before the onset of clinical symptoms of ICANS, and the increase correlated with the severity of the syndrome.

The rise in S100 levels was statistically significant compared to baseline levels both within the group and between patients with and without ICANS. Additionally, S100 levels decreased following treatment, correlating with clinical improvement.

These findings suggest that S100 may serve as a useful early marker for ICANS. However, further research, such as prospective studies, is needed to better understand the underlying mechanisms and prognostic value of S100 in this context. Nevertheless, S100 could potentially become a valuable tool for monitoring ICANS and guiding therapeutic interventions in the future.

sec.title: Statement of Ethics
sec.p: This study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval was not received for this human study because for this kind of study review by Research Ethics Committee (REC) is not mandatory in Austria. Adult participant consent was not required because this retrospective analysis was based on anonymized, preexisting, patient data, and was conducted without any direct intervention or involvement of the patients.
